title: A Thousand Gates

pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 24: A river is strong only where it is shared.*

The wind at the crater rim did not blow; it pushed. It pressed against their chests with a physical insistence, carrying a taste of iron and ice that coated the back of Wen Lan’s throat. She stood with her back to the jagged lip of the crater, the white frost in her hair stiff and bright against the dark sky. Her hands were tucked into the sleeves of her pale linen tunic to keep the cold from biting into her knuckles.

The map Shen Yu had unrolled on a flat slab of stone was not a map of the river as it had been, but of the river as it could be. It was a sprawling, intricate diagram of channels, weirs, and sluices, drawn in ink that had long since dried. Shen Yu’s hands, stained with soot and ink, trembled slightly as he tapped a point near the edge of the paper.

"Nine kilometers an hour," he said, his voice thin against the wind. He adjusted his brass-rimmed glasses, which were fogged with the cold. "That is the speed of a wave crest in open water, assuming the gradient holds. From here to the delta is two thousand kilometers." He looked up, his eyes bright with a frantic, meticulous energy. "Nine days. If every gate opens at the precise moment the wave arrives, the water does not flood. It flows. It fills the channels without surging. It is a chain reaction of pure hydraulics."

Lord Bao Heng stood beside them, his deep red silk robe snapped by the gale. He was watching the map, not Shen Yu. His face was pale, stripped of its usual soft, smiling deference. He looked, Wen thought, like a man who had been holding a heavy stone for forty years and was only now realizing that the stone was not his to keep.

"Two hundred and sixteen hours," the Lord said quietly. "Nine days." He reached out and touched a line on the map, a single thin stroke representing the main channel. "If one gate opens a minute too early, the wave breaks against the next lock. The levees crack. The valley drowns."

"It is not a minute," Wen said. She stepped forward, her boots crunching on the frost-dusted stone. "It is a heartbeat. It is the difference between a river and a flood."
pages.image: A wide panoramic view of a high-altitude crater rim where three figures stand over a large detailed map spread on stone, a young woman with a white ponytail and pale tunic, a boy with glasses and a brown vest, and an older man in a deep red silk robe, surrounded by jagged ice and thin clouds.

pages.text:
Lord Bao Heng turned from the map. The wind tore at the hem of his robe, snapping the gold thread embroidery like a loose string. He looked smaller than he had in the cistern town, smaller than he had in the letters. Here, at the roof of the world, he was just a man in expensive clothes, standing on the edge of a hole in the sky.

"My keepers will open the gates," he said. His voice was flat, stripped of its usual melodic charm. "They have waited for this command for a decade. I will send the signal. The mechanism is simple. A drum, a fire, a whistle. They will do it." He paused, and the silence stretched between them, taut as a tracker’s rope. "But they will not believe you. The people in the lower towns, the farmers, the fishermen. They have been told that the water is being stolen by the upper reaches. They have been told that you, the Bearer, are the one holding it back. They are angry, Wen Lan. They are frightened. And frightened people do not open gates. They close them."

Wen Lan felt the old heat rise in her chest, the frustration of being spoken to as if she were a problem to be solved rather than a person to be trusted. But she kept her voice level. She looked at the Lord, not with anger, but with a clear, sharp assessment.

"They are not angry because they are stupid," she said. "They are angry because they are thirsty. And because they have been lied to." She stepped closer to the map, her shadow falling across the ink lines. "You cannot command them to trust you. You cannot write a letter that tastes like water. But I can walk to them. I can stand in their fields and show them the water. I can show them that it is not a gift you are giving, but a debt you are paying."

The Lord looked at her, and for a moment his face was unreadable. Then he nodded, a slow, heavy motion. "Then that part is yours," he said. "The persuasion. The walking. The talking."

"The rest is yours," Wen replied. "The engineering. The timing. The keeping the river from eating the valley."
pages.image: A close-up of Lord Bao Heng’s pale face and hands resting on a detailed map, his deep red robe flapping in the wind, Wen Lan’s shadow falling across the paper, a young woman with a white ponytail standing in the foreground with a determined expression.

pages.text:
Auntie Mo had been silent. She stood apart from the map, her conical bamboo hat shielding her eyes, her bare feet planted firmly on the ice. She did not look at the diagrams or the calculations. Her gaze fixed on the crater, on the dark, still water that held the shape of Wen’s mother, and then on the three of them.

When she spoke, her voice was low and rough, like the scrape of a pole against a muddy bank. It cut through the wind without effort.

"A river belongs to everyone who drinks downstream," she said.

Lord Bao Heng flinched. It was a small movement, a tightening of the jaw, a sharp inhale. Wen watched it happen, and she felt a strange, cold satisfaction, not of triumph, but of recognition.

"The first ones who tried to hold the water back," Mo continued, her eyes fixed on the Lord, "were not wicked. They were not greedy. They were frightened. They saw the flood come and thought they could catch it in a net. They thought if they held it still, it would stop moving. But water does not stop. It waits. And when it moves, it takes everything it can carry."

Mo took a step forward. Her bare toes curled against the ice. "You built your cisterns because you were afraid of the dark. But the dark is not the water. The dark is the silence between the drops. You cannot drink silence, Lord Bao. You can only drink the river."

The Lord’s hand went to his mouth. He pressed his lips together, but a tear slid down his cheek, tracing a wet line through the dust on his face. He did not wipe it away. He stood there, in the howling wind, and wept. It was the quiet, exhausting sobbing of a man who has carried a weight for so long that he has forgotten it is possible to put it down.

Wen Lan watched him, and the anger in her chest dissolved, replaced by a heavy, tender pity. He was not a villain. He was a man who had tried to build a wall against the tide, and the tide had won, as it always does.

"Mo Ayi," Wen said softly.

"Yes," Mo said. She did not look at Wen. She looked at the water. "Now go. The wave does not wait for tears."
pages.image: Auntie Mo, a short woman in a blue jacket and bamboo hat, standing with her back to a large crater, her face turned toward an older man in red robes who is wiping a tear from his pale cheek, the wind blowing their clothes, a stark and emotional scene.

pages.text:
They descended the first slope of the gorge as the sun began to set, painting the ice in shades of amber and bruised purple. The air was thinner here, sharper, and every breath felt like drinking cold iron. Wen Lan walked with her boots wrapped tight, her white ponytail whipping against her back, the blue cloth tie frayed but holding.

Shen Yu walked beside her, his surveyor’s staff tapping a steady rhythm against the rock. He was quiet, his usual chatty anxiety dampened by the scale of what they were doing. He carried a small drum under his arm, a simple wooden thing with a leather head, and a bell on a long cord.

"The signal," he said, testing the weight of the drum. "It has to travel faster than the wave. If the town hears the drum before the water arrives, they have time to open the gate. If they hear it after, the gate is already flooding."

"Smoke," Wen said. She pointed to a cluster of dry brush at the edge of a path. "Burn it. Make a column. It will be visible for miles."

"A column of smoke is slow," Shen Yu said. "It drifts. The wind is against us. The drum is better. Sound travels faster than sight in this air."

"Then we do both," Wen said. "We do everything."

They walked in a line, Mo leading, her pole clicking against the stone. The Lord Bao Heng had sent a rider ahead, a young man with a red flag, to prepare the first town. The town was a cluster of stone houses built into the cliff face, dry and dusty, the fields below cracked and yellow.

When they reached the first gate, a heavy wooden structure set into the rock, Wen stopped. The gate was closed. The water behind it was still, dark, and deep.

"Open it," Wen said.

The gate-keeper, an old man with a face like dried leather, looked at her. He did not move. He looked at the Lord Bao Heng, who stood behind her, his red robe a splash of color in the grey dust.

"We have orders," the old man said. "To wait."

"To wait for what?" Wen asked.

"For the signal."

Wen looked at Mo. Mo looked at the gate. And then Mo looked at Wen, and nodded, just once.

Wen Lan stepped forward. She did not speak. She reached out and touched the wooden frame of the gate. She felt the water behind it, a cold, heavy presence, pressing against the wood. She pushed. Not with her power, but with her will. The gate groaned, the wood creaking under the strain, and then it swung open.

The water rushed out, not as a flood, but as a stream, a thin, steady ribbon of silver that hit the dry field below and began to spread.
pages.image: Wen Lan, with a white ponytail and pale tunic, standing before a large wooden gate in a rocky cliff, pushing it open, a stream of water rushing out onto dry yellow fields below, an old man in brown clothes watching with wide eyes.

pages.text:
The water hit the earth with a sound like a sigh. It spread, slow and purposeful, soaking into the cracked soil, darkening the dust, turning it into a rich, dark brown. The old gate-keeper stared at the water, his mouth open, a forgotten word on his lips.

Then, from the top of the cliff, a sound cut through the air. A whistle, shrill and clear, followed by the deep, resonant thud of a drum.

A figure appeared on the path above. It was Master Gao. He was lowering himself down the cliff on a rope and pulley that Shen Yu had rigged in a panic. He was not wearing his green silk robe. He was in a plain blue shirt, his hands raw and bleeding from the rope.

He slid down the rope and landed in the mud with a thump. He did not stand up. He stayed in the mud, breathing hard, his grey-streaked topknot disheveled. He looked at Wen, and he looked at the water, and he smiled. It was not his usual charming smile. It was the tired, relieved smile of a man who has finally put down a heavy load.

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small, brass whistle. It was the same brass whistle he had blown at the cistern. He held it up, and then, with a deliberate motion, he dropped it into the stream.

The whistle sank, and the water closed over it.

Mo Ayi said nothing. She simply leaned on her pole and watched the water flow. The drum beat again, closer this time, a steady rhythm that matched the pulse of the river.

Wen Lan watched the water spread, and she felt the frost in her hair begin to fade, just a little, as if the cold were being drawn out of her by the warmth of the earth. The river was moving. It was not a flood. It was a promise.

She turned to Shen Yu. "Next town," she said.

"Next town," he agreed.
